newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan breaks "fresh ground" in Afghan peace bid.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan breaks "fresh ground" in Afghan peace bid.

text.p: A Pakistani emissary said on Sunday he had broken fresh ground in his efforts to mediate peace in war-torn Afghanistan by holding a rare meeting with an opposition commander, Ahmad Shah Masood.

"This is a step forward as everyone seems to be willing to begin a political dialogue and this is the idea we are trying to pursue," senior Pakistan Foreign Ministry official Iftikhar Murshed told reporters after his latest talks with Afghan factions fighting the Taleban Islamic movement.

The official went to north Afghanistan on Saturday after a similar peace mission by special U.N. envoy Norbert Holl, and met Masood in the remote Farkhar valley in the northeastern province of Takhar, the official APP news agency said.

"We have broken fresh ground inasmuch as contact was established with Ahmad Shah Masood," APP quoted Murshed as telling Pakistani reporters accompanying him. "We had a good meeting with him in Takhar."

He said he also held extensive meetings with ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani and northern opposition leader General Abdul Malik in the northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif and all of them expressed confidence in Pakistan's peace efforts.

"We noted that all of them without fail have now expressed confidence in Pakistan, and what I found particularly gratifying is that they said they have great hopes in Pakistan, specially in view of the strong government we have...at the moment."
The opposition factions accuse Pakistan of helping the purist Taleban Islamic militia, which controls more than two-thirds of Afghanistan, including the capital Kabul.
Pakistan denies the charge and says it has no favourites among the warring factions, whom it helped during the guerrilla war against Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s.

Murshed, who met Afghan opposition leaders for the second time in 10 days, described as "totally positive" Pakistan's first contact with Masood, the main commander of Rabbani's ousted government, after a hiatus of about two years.
APP quoted Masood as expressing his readiness to enter into talks with other Afghan groups for the establishment of a broad-based government.
"We appreciate (Pakistani) Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's initiative for peace in our country and the Pakistan delegation has come to us with sincerity," he said.
The opposition alliance wants demilitarisation of Kabul and formation of a political commission to chart the outlines of a broad-based government.

The Taleban refuses to demilitarise Kabul, which it captured in September, and has set a ceasefire and release of its prisoners as preconditions for peace talks, which Pakistan has offered to host in Islamabad with Afghanistan's immediate neighbours as well as the United States and Russia attending.

APP quoted Masood as saying that a ceasefire was possible before the establishment of a political commission but adding: "The exchange of prisoners can only take place after an agreement is reached on basic issues."
Pakistan recognised the Taleban government in late May after the militia briefly captured Mazar-i-Sharif with Malik's help and was followed by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Malik turned on the Taleban at the end of May, linking up with a Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction to drive them from Mazar-i-Sharif after 15 hours of street fighting.
